I have been farming this land in Quzhou for 45 years, and at 67, I know every patch of my 33 mu like the back of my hand. With only my husband and me working, I cannot manage too much cotton—it is too laborious to pick—so I will keep 11 mu of cotton and put the remaining 22 mu into my reliable wheat-maize rotation, which the machines can help us harvest. My well gives me water when the rains disappoint, so I will irrigate carefully: four times for the winter wheat, three times for the summer maize, and four times for the cotton, especially when the bolls are setting. For wheat, I trust the improved varieties I have sown for years; for maize and cotton, I buy hybrid seed from the township supply store because the yield is worth the extra cost. I will apply fertilizer based on what this soil has shown me over decades—not too little, or the crop weakens, not too much, or it lodges and wastes money. The wheat already stands, so I will not disturb it with tillage now; for the maize after wheat harvest, I will run the rotary tiller quickly and plant before the soil dries; for cotton, I plough deep in spring to warm the soil and break up the clods. Pests come every year like clockwork, so wheat and maize need two sprays each, but cotton is greedy for protection—five times, or the aphids and mites will steal my lint.
